newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fashion revolution as Kinshasa changes hands.
newsitem.headline: Fashion revolution as Kinshasa changes hands.

text.p: Tommy Hilfiger isn't cool anymore in Kinshasa. Karl Kani neither. Cartier watches and crocodile loafers are also off the must-have list.

For the moment, luxury Western designer clothes and other symbols of conspicuous consumption are out -- discredited badges of the small clique that profited from Mobutu Sese Seko's regime of backhanders and official theft.
The choicest thing in town was the white rag bandana tied around the forehead to flash full support for the revolution.

In the wink of an eye on Sunday night, Kinshasa's top hotel was transformed. Out went the cell-phone, jet-setting, Reebok generation of rich kids who put up here for safety's sake as rebels took the city.

In came the soberly dressed delegation from Laurent Kabila's conquering Alliance, whose younger members favour bush hats or baseball caps, while senior officials prefer a fairly dowdy republican cloth.

At one point their paths crossed at the elevator shafts -- one lot of bags going up, the other going down, as the once privileged classes were asked to make way for the new rulers of the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire.
By Monday, workers were busily scraping off the logo Salon Zaire from the hotel's main conference room to reletter the glass with -- you've guessed it -- Salon Congo.
There is a righteous moralistic tone about the revolution which clashes with the the money-no-object boutiques in this air-conditioned isle of plenty in the middle of Kinshasa's chaotic streets.

On Monday, its corridors were choc-a-bloc, including the odd gun-toting guard in combat-stained camouflage inspecting the Breitlings, Ferragamos, silks suits, ivory statuettes and French perfume of the mall. Prices are, of course, astronomic.
Television doesn't show it much, preferring the maimed beggars, angry mobs, dead looters, open drains, hysterical crowds and victorious rebel troops of the Zaire saga.
But showy, gold-braceleted wealth was very much a part of the Mobutu regime, which had no shortage of chandeliered villas in the more salubrious quarters of Kinshasa -- and there are quite a few.

A good many of the rich have fled. The closer one was to Mobutu, the more prudent it became not to be around when the bush hats and kalashnikovs of the rebel army appeared on the horizon. But not all managed to negotiate an exit in the final hours.
In the early hours of Saturday, tanks were brought up to the hotel and Mobutu's notorious son, Kongolo, appeared in the foyer masterminding the exodus of the fleeing dictator's nearest and dearest.
The hotel was a designated rally point for foreign nationals who, in the event of an impending bloodbath, were to be rescued by a joint allied military task force on standby across the Congo river.

It became a shuttle connection for worried and rapidly departing big-wigs and their bemused wives and children. All were heavily guarded by troops still loyal to the regime in case of rebel intervention on the way to the Congo beaches where speedboats ran them to the safety of Brazzaville.
By now, they may be in Europe. But some, it seems, may find it harder to escape revolutionary justice and could be extradited by a neighbour state with an eye to future relations.
One senior voice of the rebel alliance has called for a "purge of morals" in the republic, once a byword for rampant corruption. But pragmatism is likely to prevail.
On Monday, businessmen, who almost by definition had to kow-tow to Mobutu in order to operate, were invited to meet the country's new management and the expensive loafer crowd started trickling back.
